summary: Updates RFC 6040 to clarify that its ECN propagation rules also cover IP tunnels where two IP headers are separated by a shim header. It surveys widely used tunnelling protocols with shims and updates several related RFCs.

eli5.summary: When a package is wrapped in layers, the warning sticker must be copied to the right layer. This makes sure it is, even with extra padding between layers.

questions: how does ecn work in gre tunnels
subtitle: Clarifies that ECN propagation rules cover tunnels with shim headers, and tells operators how to make older tunnel ingresses safe.

tldr.problem: RFC 6040 defined how Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) passes through IP-in-IP tunnels, but its scope was ambiguous about tunnels with shim headers (such as GRE or L2TP) between the two IP headers, and it said nothing about tunnel ingresses that do not support ECN.
tldr.mechanism: It adds scoping text to RFC 6040, requires operators to configure a non-ECN tunnel ingress to zero the outer ECN field, sets rules for fragments, and gives update text for L2TP, GRE, Teredo and AMT.
tldr.outcome: ECN markings from a congested tunnel can propagate safely, and ingresses that cannot do so clear the outer ECN field to 0b00 instead of risking broken congestion feedback loops.

today: RFC 9601 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2024. It updates RFC 6040, RFC 2661, RFC 2784, RFC 3931, RFC 4380 and RFC 7450, and no later RFC updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6040 made the rules for passing Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) through IP-in-IP tunnels consistent. Many tunnelling protocols, however, put one or more shim headers between the inner IP header and the outer IP header. Some shims are generic and wrap link-layer (L2) headers that in turn often carry IP, so the text calls the pattern 'IP-shim-(L2)-IP'.

RFC 9601 clarifies that the scope of RFC 6040 includes any IP-in-IP tunnel, including those with shims and other encapsulations between the IP headers. It updates the specifications of the relevant encapsulation protocols where needed, and it updates RFC 6040 to say how operators ought to configure a legacy tunnel ingress so that the system is not unsafe.
sections.eli5: Some tunnels wrap a packet in extra padding layers before the outer wrapper. This document says the same warning-sticker rules apply no matter how many layers are in between.

sections.title: Scope of RFC 6040 and When Propagation Is Possible
sections.content:
RFC 6040 said it covers ECN processing 'for any IP-in-IP tunnelling'. The text names two problems with that statement. First, it was meant to include shim headers between the IP headers but is ambiguous, so RFC 9601 adds text saying it applies when an outer IP header encapsulates an inner IP header either directly or indirectly, through other headers that encapsulate (or might encapsulate) the inner one.

Second, RFC 6040 is written as a specification an implementation may choose to claim compliance with. It does not cover cases where an implementation cannot reach the inner IP header, or chooses not to propagate ECN. Yet the ECN field is a non-optional part of the IP header, so any outer header must carry some value. The only safe value when the egress behaviour is unknown is to clear it to 0b00.

Propagation is often feasible when the shim and the outer header are always added or removed together (a tightly coupled shim header). Looking inside an inner Ethernet or other L2 header to find IP is strictly a layering violation, so it cannot be required, but it can be a benign optimization under the guidelines in Section 5 of RFC 9599. Propagation stays optional to implement and use, because legacy tunnels exist without ECN support, a network may be designed with no bottleneck in the tunnel, and searching inside L2 headers may cost performance.
sections.eli5: The old rule was a bit vague about tunnels with padding layers. This document says clearly that they count too, and that skipping the sticker-copying is allowed but must be done safely.

sections.title: Making a Non-ECN Tunnel Ingress Safe
sections.content:
If a tunnel egress does not implement ECN propagation, it could discard an ECN marking added inside the tunnel, which would break the ECN-based control loops that regulate load over the tunnel. So RFC 9601 updates Section 4.3 of RFC 6040. Whether or not an ingress claims compliance with RFC 6040, RFC 4301 or RFC 3168, and when the outer header is IP, the ingress MUST be configured, if possible, to zero the outer ECN field when:

  • the egress is known not to support the RFCs that define ECN propagation;
  • the egress behaviour is unknown, or an unknown egress might be dynamically paired with the ingress;
  • an IP header might be inside a non-IP header that the ingress does not inspect.

The ingress MUST NOT alter the ECN field of the arriving packet that becomes the inner header. To let operators comply, an ingress implementation MUST NOT treat the former ToS octet (IPv4) or Traffic Class octet (IPv6) as a single 8-bit field, because that conflicts with the 6-bit Diffserv field in RFC 2474 and RFC 3260. It SHOULD also be configurable to zero the outer ECN field.

Copying the ECN field as a side effect of copying the DSCP is called a seriously unsafe bug when the ingress has no ECN logic, because it never checks the egress's ECN capability.

Zeroing the outer ECN field always would be safe, but would not be enough to claim compliance with RFC 6040, which aims to introduce ECN support to tunnels.
sections.eli5: If the mail room at the far end does not understand warning stickers, the sender must peel the sticker off the outer envelope. Otherwise the far end might throw the warning away and nobody would slow down.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Reassembly
sections.content:
RFC 6040 omitted how the ECN field is handled when a tunnel fragments or reassembles packets. RFC 9601 adds three rules. If a tunnel ingress fragments a packet, it MUST set the outer ECN field of all fragments to the value it would have set had it not fragmented.

At the egress, reassembly of outer fragments follows Section 5.3 of RFC 3168 plus two extra requirements. The packet MUST be discarded if the outer ECN fields being reassembled mix Not-ECT with other ECN codepoints. If there is a mix of ECT(0) and ECT(1), the reassembled packet MUST be set to ECT(1).

The reasoning is that RFC 8311 updated RFC 3168 so ECT(1) can signal congestion-marking differences. The rule is compatible with Pre-Congestion Notification, which ranks severity from highest to lowest as Congestion Experienced (CE), ECT(1), ECT(0).
sections.eli5: If a big parcel is cut into pieces, every piece gets the same sticker. When the pieces are put back together, mixed-up stickers mean something went wrong, and the more serious of two similar stickers wins.

sections.title: Tunnel Protocols with Tightly Coupled Shims
sections.content:
RFC 9601 lists encapsulations with tightly coupled shim headers, in rough chronological order and limited to Standards Track or widely deployed protocols: PPTP, L2TPv2 and L2TPv3, GRE and NVGRE, GTP, Teredo, CAPWAP, LISP, AMT, VXLAN and VXLAN-GPE, NSH, Geneve, direct IP-in-UDP tunnelling, and TCP encapsulation of IKE and IPsec. The scope of RFC 6040 is defined in Section 3 and is not limited to this list.

Where a protocol is under IETF change control and needs ECN propagation text, update text is given. For others, implementations are RECOMMENDED to comply with RFC 6040 and their specifications to be updated to require it. Some need no change: CAPWAP already specifies RFC 3168 ECN propagation, LISP made it mandatory from the start, and Geneve already refers to RFC 6040. PPTP needs no update because L2TP replaced it as a standardized successor. VXLAN is documented in an Informational RFC, and NVGRE is a specific use of GRE, so the GRE text is intended to update NVGRE too.

Because RFC 8085 already points tunnels over UDP to RFC 6040, the scope clarification indirectly extends that guidance to shim headers, and the Section 4 rules add the previously unstated requirement that a UDP tunnel ingress clear the outer ECN field to 0b00 when the egress does not, or might not, support propagation.
sections.eli5: There are many kinds of tunnels, like different brands of delivery boxes. Some already handle stickers properly. For the rest, this document says what to do or who should fix them.

sections.title: Updates for L2TP, GRE, Teredo and AMT
sections.content:
L2TP. L2TPv2 and L2TPv3 are within the scope of RFC 6040. An operator of an LCCE without the ECN extension MUST follow the Section 4 configuration rules, and that configuration MUST be independent of the Diffserv extension of L2TP. A new ECN Capability AVP, Attribute Type 103, MAY appear in the SCCRQ and SCCRP messages. If both sides include it, they use the normal mode of RFC 6040 and copy the ECN field from inner to outer. If the terminator omits it, the initiator uses compatibility mode and clears the outer field to 0b00. Support can also be configured statically, in which case the AVP is ignored.

GRE. GRE is within scope, support for RFC 6040 is RECOMMENDED, and the operator of a GRE ingress MUST follow the Section 4 rules when the outer delivery protocol is IP. GRE has no dynamic tunnel setup of its own.

Teredo. Teredo endpoints are generally deployed on hosts, so requiring correct configuration is not feasible. Until ECN support is added to Teredo, the update says a Teredo ingress that does not support ECN propagation MUST zero the ECN field in the outer IPv6 header.

AMT. Because AMT tunnels are created dynamically, the gateway declares support with a new ECN capability flag, E, in the AMT Request Message. An E value of 1 means the sender supports RFC 6040 ECN propagation, and a gateway that does not support it MUST NOT set it. A relay that supports ECN and sees E set to 1 MUST use the normal mode toward that gateway.

IANA has assigned Attribute Type 103, named ECN Capability, in the L2TP Control Message Attribute Value Pairs registry.
sections.eli5: L2TP and AMT let the two ends ask each other 'do you understand stickers?' before copying them. For GRE and Teredo, which cannot ask, the rule is to peel the sticker off unless you know it is safe.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Security Considerations of RFC 6040 and RFC 9599 apply equally to the scope defined here. RFC 9601 adds no separate security analysis.
sections.eli5: The safety rules from the earlier documents still apply, and this one adds no new ones.
